text:
A monoatomic gas having $γ=\frac{5}{3}$ is stored in a thermally insulated container and the gas is suddenly compressed to $\left (\frac{1}{8}\right )^{\text{th}}$ of its initial volume. The ratio of final pressure and initial pressure is:

($γ$ is the ratio of specific heats of the gas at constant pressure and at constant volume)
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2025 (Online) 8th April Evening Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
To find the ratio of final pressure ($P_{f}$) to initial pressure ($P_{i}$), we use the adiabatic condition:

$P_{i}V_{i}^{γ}=P_{f}V_{f}^{γ}$

We aim to express the pressure ratio:

$\frac{P_{f}}{P_{i}}=\left (\frac{V_{i}}{V_{f}}\right )^{γ}$

Given that the final volume $V_{f}$ is $\frac{1}{8}$ of the initial volume $V_{i}$, this simplifies to:

$\left (\frac{V_{i}}{V_{f}}\right )=8$

Thus, the pressure ratio becomes:

$\frac{P_{f}}{P_{i}}=8^{\frac{5}{3}}$

Calculating $8^{\frac{5}{3}}$ gives:

$\frac{P_{f}}{P_{i}}=32$
sourceReferences: ExamSIDE explanation for JEE Main 2025 (Online) 8th April Evening Shift

text: A quantity Q is formulated as $X^{-2}Y^{+\frac{3}{2}}Z^{-\frac{2}{5}}$. X, Y, and Z are independent parameters which have fractional errors of 0.1, 0.2, and 0.5, respectively in measurement. The maximum fractional error of Q is
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2025 (Online) 8th April Evening Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
The quantity $Q$ is expressed as $Q=X^{-2}Y^{+\frac{3}{2}}Z^{-\frac{2}{5}}$. The variables $X$, $Y$, and $Z$ are independent parameters with fractional errors of 0.1, 0.2, and 0.5, respectively. To determine the maximum fractional error in $Q$, we can use the following method:

$\text{Fractional error in}Q=|-2|\frac{\Delta X}{X}+\left |\frac{3}{2}\right |\frac{\Delta Y}{Y}+\left |-\frac{2}{5}\right |\frac{\Delta Z}{Z}$

Substituting the fractional errors into the equation:

$=2\times 0.1+\frac{3}{2}\times 0.2+\frac{2}{5}\times 0.5$

Calculating each term gives:

$=0.2+0.3+0.2$

Summing these values results in:

$=0.7$

Thus, the maximum fractional error in $Q$ is 0.7.

text: For a nucleus of mass number A and radius R, the mass density of nucleus can be represented as
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2025 (Online) 8th April Evening Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
The radius $R$ of a nucleus is given by the empirical relation:

$R=r_{0}A^{\frac{1}{3}},$

where $r_{0}$ is a constant and $A$ is the mass number.

The volume $V$ of the nucleus is approximately that of a sphere:

$V=\frac{4}{3}πR^{3}.$

Substituting the expression for $R$ into the volume formula:

$V=\frac{4}{3}π\left (r_{0}A^{\frac{1}{3}}\right )^{3}=\frac{4}{3}πr_{0}^{3}A.$

The mass density $ρ$ is defined as the mass (which is proportional to $A$) divided by the volume:

$ρ=\frac{A}{V}=\frac{A}{\frac{4}{3}πr_{0}^{3}A}=\frac{1}{\frac{4}{3}πr_{0}^{3}}.$

Notice that $A$ cancels out in the numerator and denominator, so the density is:

$ρ=\text{constant},$

meaning it is independent of the mass number $A$.

Thus, the correct option is:

Option B: Independent of A.
sourceReferences: ExamSIDE explanation for JEE Main 2025 (Online) 8th April Evening Shift

[IMG]
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2025 (Online) 8th April Evening Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
The parts ABC (resistance $r$) and ADC (resistance $2r$) are in parallel, so the current divides inversely as the resistances: $i_{1}=\dfrac{2I}{3}$ through ABC and $i_{2}=\dfrac{I}{3}$ through ADC.


[IMG]

Each side is at perpendicular distance $\dfrac{a}{2}$ from the centre O and its ends subtend $45^{\circ }$ on either side of the perpendicular, so a side carrying current $i$ gives

$B_{\text{side}}=\frac{μ_{0}i}{4π(a/2)}(\sin 45^{\circ }+\sin 45^{\circ })=\frac{\sqrt{2}μ_{0}i}{2πa}$

The current in ABC goes clockwise about O and the current in ADC anticlockwise, so the fields of the two paths at O are opposite (into and out of the plane). Each path has two sides, so

$B=2\times \frac{\sqrt{2}μ_{0}}{2πa}\left (\frac{2I}{3}-\frac{I}{3}\right )=\frac{\sqrt{2}μ_{0}I}{3πa}$

Hence, the correct option is (B).

text:
The amplitude and phase of a wave that is formed by the superposition of two harmonic travelling waves, $y_{1}(x,t)=4\sin (kx-ωt)$ and $y_{2}(x,t)=2\sin (kx-ωt+\frac{2π}{3})$, are:
 (Take the angular frequency of initial waves same as $ω$)
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2025 (Online) 8th April Evening Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
Both waves have the same $k$ and $ω$. With $θ=kx-ωt$, $y_{1}=4\sin θ$ and $y_{2}=2\sin \left (θ+\dfrac{2π}{3}\right )$, so $y_{2}$ leads $y_{1}$ by $δ=\dfrac{2π}{3}=120^{\circ }$.


[IMG]

Adding the phasors of lengths 4 and 2 inclined at $120^{\circ }$, the resultant amplitude is

$A=\sqrt{A_{1}^{2}+A_{2}^{2}+2A_{1}A_{2}\cos δ}=\sqrt{16+4+2(4)(2)\left (-\dfrac{1}{2}\right )}=\sqrt{12}=2\sqrt{3}$

The phase $𝜙$ of the resultant, measured from $y_{1}$, is given by

$\tan 𝜙=\dfrac{A_{2}\sin δ}{A_{1}+A_{2}\cos δ}=\dfrac{2\times \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}}{4+2\left (-\dfrac{1}{2}\right )}=\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{3}=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\Rightarrow 𝜙=\dfrac{π}{6}$

So $y=2\sqrt{3}\sin \left (kx-ωt+\dfrac{π}{6}\right )$.

Hence, the correct option is (B).

text: A 3 m long wire of radius 3 mm shows an extension of 0.1 mm when loaded vertically by a mass of 50 kg in an experiment to determine Young's modulus. The value of Young's modulus of the wire as per this experiment is $P\times 10^{11}\text{Nm}^{-2}$, where the value of $P$ is: (Take $g=3π\text{m/s}^{2}$)
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2025 (Online) 8th April Evening Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
Let’s break down the solution step by step:

First, note the given values:

Length of the wire, $L=3\text{m}$

Radius of the wire, $r=3\text{mm}=3\times 10^{-3}\text{m}$

Extension of the wire, $\Delta L=0.1\text{mm}=1\times 10^{-4}\text{m}$

Mass attached, $m=50\text{kg}$

Acceleration due to gravity, $g=3π\text{m/s}^{2}$

The force (weight) acting on the wire is:

$F=mg=50\times 3π=150π\text{N}$

Next, calculate the cross-sectional area, $A,$ of the wire:

$A=πr^{2}=π(3\times 10^{-3})^{2}=π\times 9\times 10^{-6}=9π\times 10^{-6}\text{m}^{2}$

Young’s modulus, $E,$ is given by:

$E=\frac{FL}{A\Delta L}$

Substitute the values into the formula:

$E=\frac{(150π)\times 3}{(9π\times 10^{-6})\times (1\times 10^{-4})}$

Simplify step by step:

Multiply in the numerator:

$150π\times 3=450π$

Multiply in the denominator:

$9π\times 10^{-6}\times 1\times 10^{-4}=9π\times 10^{-10}$

Cancel the common factor $π$ in the numerator and denominator:

$E=\frac{450}{9\times 10^{-10}}$

Divide 450 by 9:

$E=\frac{450}{9}\times \frac{1}{10^{-10}}=50\times 10^{10}=5\times 10^{11}\text{Nm}^{-2}$

The problem states that Young's modulus can be expressed as $P\times 10^{11}\text{Nm}^{-2}.$ Here we have:

$P=5$

Thus, the correct option is:

Option D (5).
sourceReferences: ExamSIDE explanation for JEE Main 2025 (Online) 8th April Evening Shift

text:
Water falls from a height of 200 m into a pool. Calculate the rise in temperature of the water assuming no heat dissipation from the water in the pool.
(Take $g = 10 m/s^{2}$, specific heat of water = 4200 J/(kg K))
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2025 (Online) 8th April Evening Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
To find the rise in temperature of the water as it falls from a height, we start by equating the potential energy loss to the heat gained, assuming no heat is lost from the water in the pool.

The potential energy lost by the water can be expressed as:

$mgh$

where:

$m$ is the mass of water,

$g$ is the acceleration due to gravity (10 m/s²),

$h$ is the height (200 m).

The heat gained by the water when temperature changes is given by:

$ms\Delta T$

where:

$s$ is the specific heat capacity of water (4200 J/(kg K)),

$\Delta T$ is the change in temperature.

Setting the potential energy loss equal to the heat gained:

$mgh=ms\Delta T$

We can simplify this equation by canceling out the mass $m$:

$gh=s\Delta T$

Now, solve for $\Delta T$:

$\Delta T=\frac{gh}{s}$

Substitute the known values:

$\Delta T=\frac{10\times 200}{4200}$

Calculate $\Delta T$:

$\Delta T=\frac{2000}{4200}$

Simplify the fraction:

$\Delta T=\frac{10}{21}$

Therefore, the rise in temperature is $\Delta T\approx 0.48\text{K}$.
sourceReferences: ExamSIDE explanation for JEE Main 2025 (Online) 8th April Evening Shift

About the axis through the centre perpendicular to the plane, $I_{z}=MR^{2}$. Any two perpendicular diameters are equivalent, so by the perpendicular axis theorem $2I_{\text{dia}}=MR^{2}\Rightarrow I_{\text{dia}}=\dfrac{MR^{2}}{2}$.

$I_{\text{dia}}=\dfrac{λL}{2}\left (\dfrac{L}{2π}\right )^{2}=\dfrac{λL^{3}}{8π^{2}}$

Hence, the correct option is (A).

text: Two strings with circular cross section and made of same material, are stretched to have same amount of tension. A transverse wave is then made to pass through both the strings. The velocity of the wave in the first string having the radius of cross section R is $v_{1}$, and that in the other string having radius of cross section R/2 is $v_{2}$. Then $\frac{v_{2}}{v_{1}}$ =
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2025 (Online) 8th April Evening Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
To find the ratio of the velocities of transverse waves in two strings with different radii but identical materials and tension, consider the following:

The wave velocity $v$ in a string is given by the formula:

$v=\sqrt{\frac{T}{μ}}$

where $T$ is the tension and $μ$ is the linear mass density of the string, defined as:

$μ=ρπR^{2}$

Here, $ρ$ is the density of the material, and $R$ is the radius of the string. Given that both strings have the same tension $T$ and material, we compare their wave velocities $v_{1}$ and $v_{2}$ for radii $R_{1}=R$ and $R_{2}=\frac{R}{2}$.

The velocity ratio is expressed as:

$\frac{v_{2}}{v_{1}}=\frac{\sqrt{\frac{T}{ρπR2 2}}}{\sqrt{\frac{T}{ρπR2 1}}}$

Simplifying this expression:

$\frac{v_{2}}{v_{1}}=\frac{\sqrt{R_{1}^{2}}}{\sqrt{R_{2}^{2}}}=\frac{R_{1}}{R_{2}}=\frac{R}{\frac{R}{2}}=2$

Thus, the ratio $\frac{v_{2}}{v_{1}}$ is 2.
sourceReferences: ExamSIDE explanation for JEE Main 2025 (Online) 8th April Evening Shift

text: Two metal spheres of radius R and 3R have same surface charge density σ. If they are brought in contact and then separated, the surface charge density on smaller and bigger sphere becomes $σ_{1}$ and $σ_{2}$, respectively. The ratio $\frac{σ_{1}}{σ_{2}}$ is
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2025 (Online) 8th April Evening Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
When two conducting spheres are in contact, they achieve the same electric potential. Consider two metal spheres with radii $R$ and $3R$ that have the same surface charge density $σ$.

For a conductive sphere, the potential $V$ of a sphere can be expressed as $V=\frac{σr}{ε_{0}}$, where $r$ is the radius of the sphere and $ε_{0}$ is the permittivity of free space.

When the two spheres are brought into contact and then separated, they equalize their potentials: 

$V_{1}=V_{2}$

Thus, the equations become:

$σ_{1}r_{1}=σ_{2}r_{2}$

Substituting for the radii:

$σ_{1}R=σ_{2}(3R)$

From this, we can solve for the ratio of the surface charge densities:

$\frac{σ_{1}}{σ_{2}}=\frac{3R}{R}=3$

Therefore, the ratio of the surface charge densities on the smaller sphere to the larger sphere after contact is 3.
sourceReferences: ExamSIDE explanation for JEE Main 2025 (Online) 8th April Evening Shift

text: Two balls with same mass and initial velocity, are projected at different angles in such a way that maximum height reached by first ball is 8 times higher than that of the second ball. $T_{1}$ and $T_{2}$ are the total flying times of first and second ball, respectively, then the ratio of $T_{1}$ and $T_{2}$ is
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2025 (Online) 8th April Evening Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
Given that the maximum height reached by the first ball is 8 times that of the second ball:

$(H_{\max })_{1}=8\times (H_{\max })_{2}$

We can relate this to the initial velocities and angles using the formula for maximum height:

$\frac{u^{2}\sin ^{2}θ_{1}}{2g}=8\times \frac{u^{2}\sin ^{2}θ_{2}}{2g}$

Simplifying, we find:

$\sin θ_{1}=2\sqrt{2}\sin θ_{2}$

Now, the ratio of the total flying times $T_{1}$ and $T_{2}$ is given by:

$\frac{T_{1}}{T_{2}}=\frac{2u\sin θ_{1}/g}{2u\sin θ_{2}/g}=\frac{\sin θ_{1}}{\sin θ_{2}}=2\sqrt{2}$

Thus, the ratio of $T_{1}$ to $T_{2}$ is $2\sqrt{2}:1$.

text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion $𝐀$ and the other is labelled as Reason $𝐑$

Assertion A : Work done in moving a test charge between two points inside a uniformly charged spherical shell is zero, no matter which path is chosen.

Reason R : Electrostatic potential inside a uniformly charged spherical shell is constant and is same as that on the surface of the shell.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below.
options: A is true but R is false
Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is false but R is true
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2025 (Online) 8th April Evening Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
$\text{Assertion A:}$  

For a uniformly charged spherical shell, Gauss's law tells us that the electric field inside the shell is zero.  

Since the electric field $⃗{E}$ is zero everywhere inside, the potential $V$ must be constant.  

Work done in moving a charge from one point to another in an electric field is given by the difference in potential energy, which is $q(V_{B}-V_{A})$.  

If the potential difference $V_{B}-V_{A}$ is zero (because the potential is constant), then the work done is zero, regardless of the path taken.  

Therefore, Assertion A is true.

$\text{Reason R:}$  

It states that the electrostatic potential inside a uniformly charged spherical shell is constant and equal to that on its surface.  

This is correct because the electric field inside is zero, ensuring that the potential remains uniform inside.  

Thus, Reason R is also true.

$\text{Relationship between A and R:}$  

The work done on a test charge moving inside the shell being zero is a direct consequence of the fact that the potential is constant inside.  

Hence, Reason R correctly explains why the work done (Assertion A) is zero.

Given this analysis, the correct answer is:

Option B  

"Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A."
sourceReferences: ExamSIDE explanation for JEE Main 2025 (Online) 8th April Evening Shift

text:
An infinitely long wire has uniform linear charge density $λ=2\text{nC/m}$. The net flux through a Gaussian cube of side length $\sqrt{3}$ cm, if the wire passes through any two corners of the cube, that are maximally displaced from each other, would be $x\text{Nm}^{2}\text{C}^{-1}$, where $x$ is:

[Neglect any edge effects and use $\frac{1}{4π𝜖_{0}}=9\times 10^{9}$ SI units]
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2025 (Online) 8th April Evening Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
[IMG]

To find the net flux through a Gaussian cube when an infinitely long wire with a uniform linear charge density $λ=2\text{nC/m}$ passes through the cube's diagonal corners, we use Gauss's Law. The relevant expression is:

$𝜙=\frac{q_{\text{enc}}}{ε_{0}}$

Here, $q_{\text{enc}}$ is the charge enclosed by the Gaussian surface, and $ε_{0}$ is the permittivity of free space. 

Given:

The wire passes through two opposite corners of the cube.

The side length of the cube, $a=\sqrt{3}\text{cm}=\sqrt{3}\times 10^{-2}\text{m}$.

The length of the wire inside the cube is equal to its diagonal, which is $\sqrt{3}\times a$.

Thus, the charge enclosed $q_{\text{enc}}$ is:

$q_{\text{enc}}=λ\times \text{(length of wire inside the cube)}=λ\times \sqrt{3}\times a$

Substitute the given values:

$λ=2\times 10^{-9}\text{C/m},a=\sqrt{3}\times 10^{-2}\text{m}$

Calculating:

$q_{\text{enc}}=2\times 10^{-9}\times \sqrt{3}\times \sqrt{3}\times 10^{-2}$

Now apply Gauss's Law for net flux:

$𝜙=\frac{λ\cdot \sqrt{3}\cdot a}{ε_{0}}$

Substitute $ε_{0}=\frac{1}{4π\times 9\times 10^{9}}$:

$𝜙=2\times 10^{-9}\times \sqrt{3}\times \sqrt{3}\times 10^{-2}\times 36π\times 10^{9}$

$𝜙=2.16π\text{Nm}^{2}\text{C}^{-1}$

Thus, the net flux through the Gaussian cube is $2.16π\text{Nm}^{2}\text{C}^{-1}$.

text: A body of mass 2 kg moving with velocity of $⃗{v}_{in}=3\hat{i}+4\hat{j}\text{ms}^{-1}$ enters into a constant force field of 6N directed along positive z-axis. If the body remains in the field for a period of $\frac{5}{3}$ seconds, then velocity of the body when it emerges from force field is.
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2025 (Online) 8th April Evening Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
To determine the velocity of the body as it emerges from the force field, we can break this process down as follows:

Force and Acceleration Calculation:

The body is subjected to a constant force of 6 N, which acts along the positive z-axis. The mass of the body is 2 kg.

Using Newton's second law, $⃗{F}=m⃗{a}$, the acceleration $⃗{a}$ can be calculated as:

$⃗{a}=\frac{⃗{F}}{m}=\frac{6\hat{k}}{2}=3\hat{k}\text{ms}^{-2}$

Initial Velocity:

The initial velocity of the body is given by:

$⃗{u}=3\hat{i}+4\hat{j}\text{ms}^{-1}$

Time of Motion:

The time the body spends in the force field is:

$t=\frac{5}{3}\text{seconds}$

Final Velocity Calculation:

The final velocity $⃗{v}$ is given by the equation of motion:

$⃗{v}=⃗{u}+⃗{a}t$

Substituting the known values:

$⃗{v}=(3\hat{i}+4\hat{j})+3\hat{k}\left (\frac{5}{3}\right )$

Simplifying the expression gives:

$⃗{v}=3\hat{i}+4\hat{j}+5\hat{k}$

Therefore, the velocity of the body as it exits the force field is $3\hat{i}+4\hat{j}+5\hat{k}\text{ms}^{-1}$.
sourceReferences: ExamSIDE explanation for JEE Main 2025 (Online) 8th April Evening Shift

text: A block of mass 2 kg is attached to one end of a massless spring whose other end is fixed at a wall. The spring-mass system moves on a frictionless horizontal table. The spring's natural length is 2 m and spring constant is 200 N/m. The block is pushed such that the length of the spring becomes 1 m and then released. At distance x m (x < 2) from the wall, the speed of the block will be
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2025 (Online) 8th April Evening Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
The natural length of the spring is $2\text{m}$ and it is pushed to a length of $1\text{m}$, so the block starts from rest with a compression of $1\text{m}$.


[IMG]

At a distance $x$ from the wall ($x<2$), the compression is $(2-x)\text{m}$. The table is frictionless, so mechanical energy is conserved:

$\dfrac{1}{2}k(1)^{2}=\dfrac{1}{2}mv^{2}+\dfrac{1}{2}k(2-x)^{2}$

With $k=200\text{N m}^{-1}$ and $m=2\text{kg}$:

$v^{2}=\dfrac{k}{m}\left [1-(2-x)^{2}\right ]=100\left [1-(2-x)^{2}\right ]$

$v=10\left [1-(2-x)^{2}\right ]^{\frac{1}{2}}\text{m s}^{-1}$

Hence, the correct option is (A).

text: In a Young's double slit experiment, the source is white light. One of the slits is covered by red filter and another by a green filter. In this case:
options: there shall be alternate interference fringes of red and green.
there shall be an interference pattern for red distinct from that for green.
there shall be an interference pattern, where each fringe's pattern center is green and outer edges is red.
there shall be no interference fringes.
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2025 (Online) 8th April Evening Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
A steady interference pattern needs coherent sources: waves of the same frequency with a constant phase difference.

The red filter lets only red light through one slit and the green filter lets only green light through the other. The two waves have different frequencies, so their phase difference changes continuously with time and the interference term averages to zero; at every point the intensities simply add, $I=I_{\text{red}}+I_{\text{green}}$.

Red light emerges from only one slit and green light from only the other, so neither colour has a second coherent source to interfere with, and no red or green fringe system, alternate or separate, can form. The screen is uniformly lit by the mixture of red and green light.

Hence, the correct option is (D).
sourceReferences: ExamSIDE explanation for JEE Main 2025 (Online) 8th April Evening Shift

text:
A sample of a liquid is kept at 1 atm. It is compressed to 5 atm which leads to a change of volume of $0.8 cm^{3}$. If the bulk modulus of the liquid is 2 GPa, the initial volume of the liquid was $_______$ litre.
(Take 1 atm $= 10^{5} Pa)$
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2025 (Online) 8th April Evening Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
Given, Initial pressure of liquid $(\mathrm{P}_{\mathrm{i}})=1\mathrm{atm}$

Final pressure of liquid $(\mathrm{P}_{\mathrm{f}})=5\mathrm{atm}$

Change in pressure $(\mathrm{dP})=\mathrm{P}_{\mathrm{f}}-\mathrm{P}_{\mathrm{i}}=4\mathrm{atm}$

$=4\times 10^{5}\mathrm{Pa}$

Change in volume $(\mathrm{dV})=-0.8\mathrm{cm}^{3}$

Bulk modulus $(B)=2\times 10^{9}\mathrm{Pa}$

Now, $B=\frac{-dP}{(dV/V)}\Rightarrow V=-B\left (\frac{dV}{dP}\right )$

$\begin{array}{ll} \Rightarrow \mathrm{V} & =-2\times 10^{9}\times \dfrac{\left (-0.8\times 10^{-6}\right )}{4\times 10^{5}} \\ \qquad =4\times 10^{-3}\mathrm{m}^{3}=4\text{litre} \end{array}$
sourceReferences: ExamSIDE explanation for JEE Main 2025 (Online) 8th April Evening Shift

text: A thin solid disk of 1 kg is rotating along its diameter axis at the speed of 1800 rpm . By applying an external torque of $25π\mathrm{Nm}$ for 40 s , the speed increases to 2100 rpm . The diameter of the disk is $___________ m$.
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2025 (Online) 8th April Evening Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
Mass of the disk, $m=1\text{kg}$.

Initial angular velocity, $ω_{i}=1800\text{rpm}$.

Final angular velocity, $ω_{f}=2100\text{rpm}$.

External torque, $τ_{\text{ext}}=25π\text{Nm}$.

Time, $t=40\text{seconds}$.

First, convert the rotational speeds from revolutions per minute (rpm) to radians per second (rad/s):

$ω_{i}=1800\times \frac{2π}{60}=60π\text{rad/s}$

$ω_{f}=2100\times \frac{2π}{60}=70π\text{rad/s}$

Next, use the equation of motion for rotation to find the angular acceleration $α$:

$ω_{f}=ω_{i}+αt$

$70π=60π+α(40)$

Solving for $α$:

$α=\frac{70π-60π}{40}=\frac{10π}{40}=\frac{π}{4}\text{rad/s}^{2}$

The torque and moment of inertia relationship is given by:

$τ=Iα$

For a thin solid disk rotating along its diameter, the moment of inertia $I$ is $\frac{mR^{2}}{4}$. Thus:

$25π=\frac{1\times R^{2}}{4}\times \frac{π}{4}$

Solving for $R$:

$25π=\frac{πR^{2}}{16}$

$R^{2}=\frac{25π\times 16}{π}=400$

$R=20\text{m}$

The diameter of the disk is:

$\text{Diameter}=2R=2\times 20=40\text{m}$
sourceReferences: ExamSIDE explanation for JEE Main 2025 (Online) 8th April Evening Shift

text: An electron is released from rest near an infinite non-conducting sheet of uniform charge density '$-σ$'. The rate of change of de-Broglie wave length associated with the electron varies inversely as $n^{th}$ power of time. The numerical value of n is $_____$.
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2025 (Online) 8th April Evening Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
An infinite sheet of charge density $-σ$ produces a uniform field of magnitude $E=\dfrac{σ}{2ε_{0}}$, so the electron (charge $-e$) is repelled with constant acceleration

$a=\dfrac{eE}{m}=\dfrac{eσ}{2mε_{0}}$

Starting from rest, its momentum after time $t$ is $p=mat=\dfrac{eσt}{2ε_{0}}$.

The de Broglie wavelength is

$λ=\dfrac{h}{p}=\dfrac{2ε_{0}h}{eσt}$

$\dfrac{dλ}{dt}=-\dfrac{2ε_{0}h}{eσt^{2}}\propto \dfrac{1}{t^{2}}$

The rate of change of the wavelength varies inversely as the second power of time, so $n=2$.

Hence, the answer is 2.
sourceReferences: ExamSIDE explanation for JEE Main 2025 (Online) 8th April Evening Shift
